title: How Much Money Do MLM Participants Actually Make?

scenes.purpose: Land the viewer in a familiar moment before any data.

visual.description: A phone on a dark table, screen off. It lights with one message notification; the sender's name and preview are soft-blurred so nothing is legible. Slow push-in. No on-screen text.

scenes.direction: Open cold, no music sting; ambient room tone.
scenes.narration: Somewhere in your messages there is probably a pitch like this.

scenes.purpose: Show the two income streams the pitch promises without stating any figure.

visual.description: The message opens into a chat bubble; from it a simple node diagram grows: a circle labelled YOU, an arrow in from 'what you sell', then a second tier of circles beneath you with arrows flowing up labelled 'what they sell'. The second tier draws in as the narration reaches 'everyone you bring in after you'.

scenes.narration: A friend you have not heard from in years has started a business, and she would love to have you on her team: you earn from what you sell, and from everyone you bring in after you.

scenes.purpose: The pitch's own word for the promise, in a recruiter's words.

visual.description: Quote card: the quoted words type on in large serif over the dark field; the word 'leverage' holds and turns amber as the sentence ends. Beneath, small: 'recruiting training video'. No channel name or face.
onScreenText: "finally create the leverage that you need inside of your network marketing business"

citations.label: Network-marketing recruiting video (YouTube)

scenes.narration: The recruiters have a word for that second part: one trainer, Frazer Brookes, promises to show you how to "finally create the leverage that you need inside of your network marketing business".

scenes.purpose: The first hard number lands against the pitch.

visual.description: Big-number reveal: '601' counts up in grotesque numerals with 'asked in 2018' beneath. Then a single horizontal bar splits left to right into three segments: 47% lost money (red), 27% broke even (slate), 25% made any profit (muted green). The 47% segment fills first, with the narration; the 25% segment fills last, on 'only 25 percent'.

chart.title: Profit or loss over their whole time in the MLM
chart.note: Self-reported. One bar, three segments; no distribution within segments is shown here (sc21 and sc22 carry the bands).

scenes.direction: Cut on the beat; let the 47% sit for a second before 27% and 25% fill.
scenes.narration: In a study published in 2018, AARP asked 601 Americans who had actually done this how it went, and 47 percent said they lost money. Only 25 percent said they made any profit at all.

scenes.purpose: Pose the question the video answers.

visual.description: The bar from sc04 shrinks to a thin line at the top; the question types on in two lines: 'Where does the money go?' / 'Why does leverage show up in almost nobody's bank account?'. Amber cursor blinks.

scenes.direction: Hold the question through a one-second pause, then title card.
scenes.narration: So where does the money go, and why does leverage that sounds so good on paper show up in almost nobody's bank account?

scenes.purpose: Title card.

visual.description: Title card: 'How much money do MLM participants actually make?' set large; under it a thin rule and the word 'evidence' in the slate accent.
onScreenText: How much money do MLM participants actually make?

scenes.direction: Simple fade; 2 s hold is covered by the narration.
scenes.narration: This video is about one question: how much money do people in multi-level marketing actually make?

scenes.purpose: Introduce the three kinds of evidence as three objects the viewer will see again.

visual.description: Three cards slide in left to right as each is named: a stack of documents labelled 'income disclosures, 70 statements, read by FTC staff'; a grid of people icons labelled 'survey, 601 participants, AARP'; a spreadsheet icon labelled '30 companies, Jon Taylor (critic)'. The cards persist as a small legend in later scenes.

citations.label: FTC staff report on MLM income disclosure statements (70 statements)
AARP, 2018 survey of 601 current and former MLM participants
J. M. Taylor, The Case (for and) against Multi-level Marketing, ch. 7

scenes.narration: To answer it we have the companies' own numbers first: 70 income disclosure statements, read closely by Federal Trade Commission staff. Then a nationally representative survey of 601 participants by AARP. And an analysis of 30 companies by Jon Taylor, an independent analyst who argues against the industry.

scenes.purpose: The pitch in three voices, each a card, none a face.

visual.description: Three quote cards in sequence, each sliding up and settling: 'it starts to compound' with a small snowball glyph rolling; 'might recruit 10 people themselves and have an organization of a thousand people' with the node tree growing one tier behind the text; 'better to have a smaller percentage of 100 people than 100 of yourself'. Attribution lines read 'recruiting coach', 'recruiting trainer', 'network-marketing trainer' in small type.
onScreenText: "might recruit 10 people themselves and have an organization of a thousand people"
"better to have a smaller percentage of 100 people than 100 of yourself"

citations.label: Recruiting coach video (YouTube)
Recruiting trainer video (YouTube)
Network-marketing trainer video (YouTube)

scenes.direction: Quotes are the only amber elements on screen; keep the tree animation subdued behind the second card.
scenes.narration: First, the promise, in the recruiters' own words: one coach, Darin Kidd, tells his audience that once the team grows, "it starts to compound", like a snowball; Frazer Brookes says the person you bring in "might recruit 10 people themselves and have an organization of a thousand people". Another trainer, Eric Worre, puts the whole idea in one line: it would be "better to have a smaller percentage of 100 people than 100 of yourself".

scenes.purpose: Name the promise in one picture: money flowing up a tree.

visual.description: The node tree from sc02, three tiers, with small coin glyphs travelling up the arrows toward the top node. Caption in amber: 'income from the efforts of others'.
onScreenText: income from the efforts of others

scenes.narration: That is the pitch: income from the efforts of other people.

scenes.purpose: The critics' version and the regulator's consumer page, as plain cards.

visual.description: Two cards in the slate accent: 'You make money from signing people up.' attributed 'Last Week Tonight'; then a browser-window frame with the FTC consumer page's sentence set in its own plain type: 'Most people who join legitimate MLMs make little or no money.' with the URL path shown small.
onScreenText: "You make money from signing people up."
"Most people who join legitimate MLMs make little or no money."

citations.label: Last Week Tonight, MLM segment (HBO)
FTC consumer advice: Multi-Level Marketing Businesses and Pyramid Schemes

scenes.narration: The critics have their own one-liner; in a clip John Oliver's show played, a former Herbalife distributor puts it this way: "You make money from signing people up." Even the FTC's own Consumer Advice page says, flatly, that "Most people who join legitimate MLMs make little or no money."

scenes.purpose: A beat before the investigation.

visual.description: Split field: amber 'the pitch' left, slate 'the critics' right; both wipe to black from the centre as the data section begins.

scenes.direction: Wipe over the last two words.
scenes.narration: Two confident stories, so let us see which one the numbers tell.

scenes.purpose: Make the disclosures a physical thing: seventy documents.

visual.description: A grid of 70 small document thumbnails (generic, no logos) tiles in, counting up in the corner to 70. One thumbnail enlarges into the FTC summary passage with the phrase highlighted.

citations.label: FTC staff report on MLM income disclosure statements (70 statements)

scenes.narration: Start with the companies, because some of them publish an income disclosure statement, and FTC staff collected 70 of them, from household names to small firms.

scenes.purpose: The headline figures as published.

visual.description: Three stat tiles, revealed in order with the narration: '$1,000 or less a year' (most participants), 'under $84 a month', '17 of 70: most participants made nothing'. The third tile turns red as it lands.
onScreenText: most participants: $1,000 or less a year
17 of 70 companies: most participants made nothing

FTC staff report, section X (27 disclosures giving the no-income share)

scenes.narration: Once FTC staff worked through the fine print, the statements with enough data to tell showed most participants received $1,000 or less in a year: under $84 a month. In at least 17 of the 70 companies, most participants made nothing at all.

scenes.purpose: Signal the turn: now the fine print.

visual.description: Camera pushes into the bottom of a disclosure thumbnail until a block of tiny footnote text fills the frame, blurred just enough to be unreadable; the words 'three things' type over it in amber.
onScreenText: three things in the fine print

scenes.narration: And that is the generous reading, because of three things buried in the fine print.

scenes.purpose: Show the denominator trick: zero-earners leave the table before the average is taken.

visual.description: A 10 by 10 grid of person icons labelled 'participants'. A dotted frame labelled 'the table' encloses the grid. On '29 leave out', the icons marked with a '$0' tag fade and slide outside the frame; on 'another 24', icons tagged 'inactive' follow. A bar labelled 'average' at the right rises visibly as they leave, with no numeral on it. Counters: '29 of 70 statements exclude non-earners', '24 of 70 exclude "inactive" participants'.
onScreenText: 29 of 70 statements leave out participants with no commission

citations.label: FTC staff report, section IV (who is excluded)

scenes.direction: The average bar rises without a value: the point is direction, not magnitude.
scenes.narration: First, who gets counted: of the 70 statements, 29 leave out participants who earned no commission, and another 24 leave out anyone the company has labelled inactive. What happens to an average when you remove the zeros before you take it?

scenes.purpose: Payout is not profit: show the missing expense block without inventing its size.

visual.description: A waterfall sketch: one solid bar labelled 'paid by the company'. To its right a hatched block labelled 'expenses: not reported' drops from the top of the bar with a question mark for its height; the result bar is drawn as a dashed outline labelled 'what you keep: unknown'. Counters: 'none of 70 statements: income after all expenses', '20 of 70: expenses not mentioned'.
onScreenText: none of the 70 statements reports income after all expenses

citations.label: FTC staff report, section V (expenses)

scenes.direction: The hatched block must read as unknown height; never give it a number.
scenes.narration: Second, what gets counted: not one of the 70 statements reports income with expenses taken out in full, and 20 of them never say whether expenses were taken out at all. So the dollar figures are what the company paid out, before most or all of whatever the participant spent to take part.

scenes.purpose: The presentation trick, in the FTC's own words.

visual.description: The FTC passage on rank tables, set as a document page; the phrase highlights in slate as it is spoken, then the words 'two or three lowest ranks' highlight.

citations.label: FTC staff report, section VIII (rank tables)

scenes.narration: Third, how it is presented: 44 of the 70 break the numbers out only by rank, and in those tables, nearly without exception, the vast majority of participants sit in the two or three lowest ranks.

scenes.purpose: The single most revealing visual: one rank table drawn two ways.

visual.description: Left: the table 'as the company shows it', ten equal rows, average earnings in the right column. Right: 'as the people are distributed', the same ten rows but each row's height proportional to its share of participants, so the $41.69 row fills 92% of the height and the top five rows are hairlines. The right panel builds row by row from the bottom; the $1,018,350.20 row is marked with a magnifier callout because it is too thin to see. Final overlay: 'half the rows describe half of one percent of participants'.
onScreenText: half the rows describe half of one percent of the people

chart.title: One income disclosure table, excerpted by the FTC (Figure 6)

citations.label: FTC staff report, Figure 6: excerpted data from one income disclosure table

scenes.direction: Hold the proportional view 1.5 s after the last word.
scenes.narration: One table the FTC excerpted shows the shape: 92.37 percent of participants in the bottom row, with average earnings of $41.69. The top row averages just over $1,018,350, and holds fewer than 0.01 percent of participants; as the FTC puts it, half the rows in that table describe half a percent of the people.

scenes.purpose: Pivot from payouts to profit.

visual.description: Two words on the field: 'paid out' (slate, left) and 'came out ahead' (amber, right) with a thin arrow between; the left word dims as the narration says 'ask the people'.

scenes.narration: Disclosures count what companies paid, not whether anyone came out ahead; for that you have to ask the people.

scenes.purpose: The survey's headline split, as people.

visual.description: A field of 601 small dots arranges into a rectangle labelled 'nationally representative sample, 2018'. The dots recolour by group with the narration: 47% red (lost money), 27% slate (broke even), 25% muted green (made a profit); a legend with the three percentages appears at the right.

chart.title: Profit or loss over their whole time in the MLM, self-reported
chart.note: Dot counts are proportional (601 dots); do not label individual dots with dollar values.

citations.label: AARP, 2018 survey of 601 current and former MLM participants

scenes.narration: AARP did, in a study published in 2018, using a probability-based national panel, the kind of sample that lets you generalise to the whole country. Among the 601 people it reached, 47 percent said they lost money, 27 percent said they broke even, and the rest, a quarter, said they made a profit, counting their entire time in the business.

scenes.purpose: What profit meant: the bands, with the top as three people.

visual.description: Zoom into the green 25%: a horizontal bar chart of profit bands as a share of all 601 participants: under $5,000 (14%), $5,000 to $9,999 (6%), $10,000 to $24,999 (3%), $25,000 or more (3%). Then three single dots lift out of the last band with the caption '3 people (half of one percent): $100,000 or more; each more than five years in; one founded the company'.

chart.title: Reported profit, share of all 601 participants
chart.note: Shares are of all participants, not of profit-makers; the $100,000 group is three individuals and must be drawn as three dots, not a bar.

citations.label: AARP, 2018 survey of 601 current and former MLM participants

scenes.direction: The three dots are the emotional beat; give them a second.
scenes.narration: Profit, for most of that quarter, was small, and so were most of the losses: on both sides of the ledger the commonest outcome was under $5,000. Only three people in the whole sample reported profits of $100,000 or more, and one of them had founded the company.

scenes.purpose: The loss side, mirrored in the chart the narration no longer reads aloud, then the self-report caveat stamped on it.

visual.description: The same bar layout mirrored to the left in red: lost under $5,000 (41%), $5,000 to $9,999 (3%), more than $10,000 (1%). As s65 begins, a stamp reads 'self-reported' across both charts, and a small tag 'profit or loss, not payout' appears beneath.

chart.title: Reported loss, share of all 601 participants
chart.note: Self-reported totals over the whole time in the MLM.

citations.label: AARP, 2018 survey of 601 current and former MLM participants

scenes.narration: These are people's own accounts of what they put in and took out, which is a limit; they are also the only figures so far that measure profit or loss rather than payout.

scenes.purpose: Turn to mechanism.

visual.description: The question 'why doesn't it compound?' types on; the snowball glyph from sc08 rolls in and stops.

scenes.narration: So most people lose or break even, and the few who profit mostly profit a little. The pitch said recruiting would compound, so why doesn't it?

scenes.purpose: How the pay plans pay, as three icons and one dashed one.

visual.description: Three solid icons appear in a row as named: 'buy a set amount of product', 'get others to buy it', 'recruit people who buy it', each with a coin arrow to a 'commission' node. A fourth icon, 'sell to an outside customer at a markup', is drawn dashed and labelled 'in some cases' in the FTC's words.

citations.label: FTC staff report, section I (how MLMs pay)

scenes.narration: The FTC describes how the pay plans typically work: commissions for hitting benchmarks such as buying a set amount of product, getting others to buy it, or recruiting people who then buy it; selling to an outside customer at a markup is mentioned as a source of income "in some cases".

scenes.purpose: Taylor's conclusion in his words, then the FTC's limit.

visual.description: Taylor's page, with the sentence highlighted in amber as it is read; then the page dims and a caption in slate: 'the FTC describes the structure; neither document measures the split between downline and retail income'.
onScreenText: 30 companies with earnings data; 350 plans reviewed

excerpt.highlight: rewards are paid primarily for the aggressive recruitment of a large downline, not for retailing products

citations.label: J. M. Taylor, The Case (for and) against Multi-level Marketing, ch. 7
FTC staff report, section I

scenes.narration: Taylor went further: he read the compensation plans of the 30 companies with published earnings data, and of more than 350 in all, and concluded that each of them pays primarily for recruiting a large downline rather than for retailing product, with most of the payout going to the highest levels. That is one analyst's reading of the plans; the FTC's report describes the same structure but does not measure how much income actually comes from downlines versus retail customers.

scenes.purpose: The recruiters' rebuttal, and why both can be true.

visual.description: Quote card in amber: the trainer's sentence. Then the node tree returns; a label 'customer' slides onto one of the recruit nodes, which is also holding a product box, and a coin arrow rises from it to the node above.
onScreenText: "you don't get paid for the act of building the team you only get paid when sales happen to a customer"
the customer is often the recruit

citations.label: Network-marketing trainer video (YouTube)
FTC staff report, section I

scenes.narration: The recruiters reject that framing; the same trainer insists that "you don't get paid for the act of building the team you only get paid when sales happen to a customer". Both can be true at once, because in the plans the FTC describes, the "customer" can be the recruit, buying a set amount of product to qualify, and the plans pay commissions on those purchases.

scenes.purpose: Who the downline is: the bottom of the tree lights up.

visual.description: The node tree expands to many tiers; the bottom tier floods the frame and is tinted red with a label 'over 90% of participants, average under $100 (one excerpted table)'. The top node is a single amber point.

citations.label: FTC staff report, Figure 6 (one disclosure's rank table)

scenes.narration: Which brings us back to leverage: if income flows up from a downline, somebody has to be the downline. In that rank table, over 90 percent of participants were in a cohort averaging under $100.

scenes.purpose: The pitch's own phrase, from a critic's summary of it.

visual.description: Taylor's two-column page; the right-hand column is lifted out and set cleanly, with 'time freedom or leveraged income' highlighted in amber.

citations.label: J. M. Taylor, The Case (for and) against Multi-level Marketing, ch. 7

scenes.narration: Taylor's own summary of the pitch says the quiet part: the appeal is "time freedom or leveraged income", a flow from the efforts of others, and under these pay plans getting it depends on recruiting a downline more than on selling the product.

scenes.purpose: Taylor's estimate as a thousand people, with its assumption printed on it.

visual.description: A grid of 1,000 small squares fills the frame; 996 turn red one row at a time, 4 stay green. Labels: '99.6% lose money', '1 in 238 profit'. On s42 a slate caption prints across the top: 'estimate from company tables, under stated assumptions about required purchases and expenses'.

chart.title: Taylor's calculated loss rate across 30 MLMs
chart.note: A calculation under Taylor's assumptions, not a measurement; the caption is part of the chart, not optional.

citations.label: J. M. Taylor, The Case (for and) against Multi-level Marketing, ch. 7, Appendix 7A

scenes.narration: His own estimate is blunter: across those companies, after subtracting required purchases and modest expenses, he puts the share losing money at 99.6 percent, about one in 238 profiting. That number depends on his assumptions about what participants had to spend, how many dropped out and how many were ever counted, which he states; it is an estimate built on the companies' tables, not a measurement of anyone's bank account.

scenes.purpose: The critics' arithmetic, labelled as theirs.

visual.description: A pyramid of dots grows level by level, each level several times the last, until it overflows a small outline of the globe at the bottom of the frame; a counter at the side ticks levels up to 13. Label in slate: 'the critics' arithmetic (Last Week Tonight)'.

citations.label: Last Week Tonight, MLM segment (HBO)

scenes.direction: Keep it playful; this is a thought experiment and the next scene says so.
scenes.narration: Critics like to finish with arithmetic; in John Oliver's version, if each recruit brings in a handful more, "you could only do that 13 cycles and you would exceed the population of the earth."

scenes.purpose: What is tested and what is not: saturation as people's reasons for leaving.

visual.description: Caption first: 'not tested by any study here'. Then two bars from the survey's reasons for leaving: 'the commission structure mostly benefited those at the top' 29%, 'the market was too saturated' 25%. Taylor's phrase 'recruitment will dry up as the market becomes saturated' sits beneath in small serif.
onScreenText: 29%: left because the structure benefited those at the top
25%: left because the market was saturated
not tested by any study here

chart.title: Reasons former participants gave for leaving (AARP)

points.label: commission structure mostly benefited those at the top

chart.note: Self-reported reasons among former participants; not a structural test.

citations.label: AARP, 2018 survey of 601 current and former MLM participants
J. M. Taylor, The Case (for and) against Multi-level Marketing, ch. 7

scenes.narration: None of the studies here tests that arithmetic directly; what they show is the shape it predicts. Taylor writes of pyramid schemes, a class in which he places MLMs, that recruitment eventually dries up as the market saturates, leaving the vast majority at the bottom. And among the former participants AARP surveyed, 29 percent said they left because the commission structure mostly benefited those at the top, and 25 percent because the market was saturated.

scenes.purpose: Section break into findings.

visual.description: Title: 'three measures, one shape'. The three evidence cards from sc07 line up beneath.

scenes.narration: Put the three side by side and they agree on the shape, though they measure different things.

scenes.purpose: The three answers side by side, each labelled with what it measures.

visual.description: Three panels. Left, 'company payouts': '$1,000 or less a year' with 'before expenses; non-earners often excluded' beneath. Middle, 'survey, profit or loss': the 47 / 27 / 25 stacked bar with '14% of participants made under $5,000'. Right, 'analyst's estimate': '99.6% lose' with 'required purchases counted as cost' beneath.
onScreenText: payouts: $1,000 or less a year, before expenses

chart.title: Three measures of the same question
chart.note: Each panel is labelled with its measure; they are not the same quantity and must not be drawn on one axis.

citations.label: FTC staff report on MLM income disclosure statements (70 statements)
AARP, 2018 survey of 601 current and former MLM participants
J. M. Taylor, The Case (for and) against Multi-level Marketing, ch. 7

scenes.narration: The companies' own statements: most participants received $1,000 or less in a year, before expenses, and most of the tables leave some participants out entirely. The survey: 47 percent lost, 27 percent broke even, a quarter profited, mostly under $5,000; the analyst: 99.6 percent losing, once required purchases are counted as a cost.

scenes.purpose: Limits, stated plainly, as a list that builds.

visual.description: A plain list in slate builds one line per clause: 'self-reported'; 'current and former participants'; 'payouts, not profit'; '70 companies whose statements were public'. The three evidence cards sit faintly behind.

citations.label: AARP, 2018 survey of 601 current and former MLM participants
FTC staff report on MLM income disclosure statements (70 statements)

scenes.narration: Now the limits, because they matter: the AARP numbers are self-reported, by current and former participants, and nothing checks them against bank statements. The FTC's figures are company payouts, not profit, and they cover the 70 companies whose statements were publicly available, which is not the whole industry.

scenes.purpose: Limits, continued.

visual.description: The list continues: 'a critic's calculation under stated assumptions'; 'recruiting vs retail income: described, not measured'; 'the thirteen-cycles arithmetic: untested'. The last line gets a small pyramid glyph with a question mark.
onScreenText: recruiting vs retail income: described, not measured

citations.label: J. M. Taylor, The Case (for and) against Multi-level Marketing, ch. 7
FTC staff report, section I

scenes.narration: Taylor is an independent analyst who argues against the industry, and his 99.6 percent is a calculation under assumptions he states, not a count of real accounts. The split between recruiting income and retail income has been described in these documents, and argued, but not measured. And the population arithmetic is a thought experiment that none of these studies tested; the rank tables show where people end up, not why.

scenes.purpose: Return to the opening moment.

visual.description: The phone from sc01, now in hand; the reply box is open with a blinking cursor; nothing typed.

scenes.narration: So, back to that message from your friend; suppose you say yes.

scenes.purpose: The base rates a viewer can carry away.

visual.description: The 47 and 27 segments from sc04 merge into one bar labelled '74%: lost money or broke even'; the remaining 25% segment opens to show 'most profits under $5,000'. The figure 74% is drawn as the sum of the two segments, with '47 + 27' faintly beneath.
onScreenText: if you profit: most likely under $5,000

chart.title: Most likely outcomes, from the AARP survey
chart.note: 74% is the sum of the first two segments (shown as 47 + 27); it is a base rate, not a prediction for one person.

citations.label: AARP, 2018 survey of 601 current and former MLM participants
AARP, 2018 survey of 601 current and former MLM participants

scenes.narration: The survey says the most likely outcome, by a wide margin, is that you lose money or break even: 74 percent of participants did. If you do profit, the same survey suggests it will most likely be under $5,000 over your whole time in the business.

scenes.purpose: Leverage, located.

visual.description: The node tree, full height; the single top node pulses amber; the base stays red.
onScreenText: it exists; here is who it works for

scenes.narration: And the leverage? It exists, in the plan documents; the rank tables show who it works for.

scenes.purpose: A checklist the viewer can use.

visual.description: A disclosure-statement outline with three callouts appearing in turn: 'who is left out of the table?', 'are the figures before expenses?', 'how many people are in the bottom row?'. Bullets, no numerals.
onScreenText: who is left out of the table?
how many people are in the bottom row?

scenes.direction: Each callout lands with its clause.
scenes.narration: Before you answer, ask for the income disclosure statement, and then ask three questions of it: who is left out of the table, whether the figures are before expenses, and how many people are in the bottom row.

scenes.purpose: Answer the title question with the numbers already shown.

visual.description: A closing composite: the 47 / 27 / 25 ring (survey) at left; '$1,000 or less a year, before expenses' (disclosures) at right; beneath, a line of three dots labelled 'half of one percent: $100,000 or more'.
onScreenText: $1,000 or less a year, before expenses

chart.title: How much do MLM participants make?
chart.note: Repeat of earlier figures only; nothing new is introduced here.

citations.label: AARP, 2018 survey of 601 current and former MLM participants
FTC staff report on MLM income disclosure statements (70 statements)
AARP, 2018 survey of 601 current and former MLM participants

scenes.narration: How much money do MLM participants actually make? For most of them, nothing, or less than nothing: in the nationally representative survey, 47 percent lost money and 27 percent broke even, and in the companies' own statements most participants received $1,000 or less in a year before expenses. A quarter made some profit, mostly small, and half of one percent made a lot.

scenes.purpose: The promise, resolved.

visual.description: The node tree one last time: the top point amber, the base red, a thin label 'more than 90%' along the base and 'the fraction at the top' by the point.
onScreenText: real for the fraction at the top

citations.label: FTC staff report, Figure 6 (one disclosure's rank table)
J. M. Taylor, The Case (for and) against Multi-level Marketing, ch. 7

scenes.narration: The leverage the pitch sells is real for the fraction at the top; in the plans Taylor read, most of the payout goes to the highest levels, and in the FTC's rank tables the vast majority sit at the bottom.

scenes.purpose: End on the person, not the data.

scenes.narration: None of that is a verdict on your friend. It is a description of the structure she has joined, written mostly by the companies themselves, and it is worth reading before you join it too.
